```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5)

beetles <- read.csv("../../data/BeetleFumigation.csv")
x <- beetles$log10_dose
n_exposed <- beetles$beetles
killed <- beetles$killed

nll_ab <- function(a, b, xx = x) {
  -sum(dbinom(killed, size = n_exposed, prob = plogis(a + b * xx), log = TRUE))
}
fit <- optim(c(-60, 34), function(p) nll_ab(p[1], p[2]), method = "BFGS",
             hessian = TRUE, control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-12))
fit_c <- optim(c(1, 34), function(p) nll_ab(p[1], p[2], x - 1.8), method = "BFGS",
               hessian = TRUE, control = list(reltol = 1e-12))
a_hat <- fit$par[1]
b_hat <- fit$par[2]
lr_cut <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2

b_seq <- seq(26, 43, by = 0.005)
prof_b <- sapply(b_seq, function(b) optimize(function(a) nll_ab(a, b), c(-95, -30))$objective)
slice_b <- sapply(b_seq, function(b) nll_ab(a_hat, b))
prof_int <- range(b_seq[prof_b <= fit$value + lr_cut])
slice_int <- range(b_seq[slice_b <= fit$value + lr_cut])

# centered Hessian as printed in the handout
h_aa <- 58.5; h_ab <- -1.26; h_bb <- 0.145
se1_c <- 1 / sqrt(h_bb)
r_c <- -h_ab / sqrt(h_aa * h_bb)
se2_c <- se1_c / sqrt(1 - r_c^2)
b_used <- round(b_hat, 2)
int1_c <- b_used + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se1_c
int2_c <- b_used + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se2_c

# uncentered values as printed in 2b
se1_u <- 1 / sqrt(185)
se2_u <- se1_u / sqrt(1 - 0.99968^2)
int1_u <- b_used + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se1_u
int2_u <- b_used + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se2_u
se_exact <- sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian)))[2]
r_exact_u <- cov2cor(solve(fit$hessian))[1, 2]
r_exact_c <- cov2cor(solve(fit_c$hessian))[1, 2]
ld50_log <- -a_hat / b_hat

f2 <- function(v, d = 2) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = d)
```

Each item repeats the handout's question, then gives the answer, a
short rationale, and mistakes to watch for. Questions with one correct
answer are answered directly. Open-ended items (the "which is honest"
part of 1a, the explanation in 1b, the judgment part of 2a, and the last
part of 2b) get sample answers or discussion points instead. All
numbers are computed in R when this file is knitted.

Model: killed$_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n_i, p_i)$ with
$\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} = a + b x_i$, $x_i$ = log10 dose. MLEs:
$\hat a = `r f2(a_hat)`$, $\hat b = `r f2(b_hat)`$. The whole Act is
pen and paper; students read values off the printed figures and use a
calculator for Part 2.

## Part 1: The likelihood surface

**1a.**

> Estimate two intervals for $b$ by eye from the figure (rough values
> are fine). The **slice** interval: hold $a$ at $\hat a$ and find the
> range of $b$ that stays inside the thick curve. The **profile**
> interval: the full range of $b$ values the thick curve reaches. Which
> interval is honest, and why?
>
> Slice: ____ to ____ Profile: ____ to ____

**Answer.** Slice: about `r f2(slice_int[1])` to `r f2(slice_int[2])`
(by eye, "about 34.3, basically a single point" is a full-credit
answer). Profile: about `r f2(prof_int[1], 1)` to
`r f2(prof_int[2], 1)` (anything from roughly 28-29 to 40-41 is fine).
The profile interval is the honest one.

**Why.** The slice asks how far $b$ can move with $a$ frozen at
$\hat a$. Because the valley is so thin and tilted, $b$ can barely move
before the fit gets much worse. But $a$ is uncertain too; if $b$
changes, $a$ can change with it and the fit stays good. The profile lets
$a$ adjust for every value of $b$, which is what the extreme top and
bottom points of the thick curve represent.

**Watch for.** Reading the slice as the width of the whole ellipse
along some diagonal. Students who say the slice is honest "because it
uses the best $a$" have missed that $\hat a$ is itself uncertain; this is
the misconception to target in the group discussion.

**1b.**

> The intercept $a$ is the log-odds of death at what dose (as $x$, and
> in mg/L)? Use your answer to explain why the valley is a long, thin
> diagonal: why does every good fit with a steeper slope also need a more
> negative intercept?

**Answer.** $a$ is the log-odds of death at $x = 0$, a dose of
$10^0 = 1$ mg/L, far below the tested doses (49-77 mg/L). Every good fit
has to pass through roughly 50% mortality near the middle of the data
($x \approx `r f2(ld50_log)`$). A line that stays near that point but gets
steeper must drop further by the time it reaches $x = 0$, so a larger
$b$ needs a more negative $a$.

**Why.** At the LD50, $a + b\,x_{50} = 0$, so $a = -b\,x_{50}$. Along
the valley, a change in $b$ is matched by a change in $a$ about
$`r f2(ld50_log)`$ times as large in the opposite direction, which is
the slope of the thick curve on the figure. Because $x = 0$ is so far
from the data, a tiny change in $b$ swings $a$ a long way, which is why
the valley is so long and thin.

**Watch for.** Answering "at the lowest dose tested." Some students say
"$a$ has no biological meaning" and stop; push them to say where
$x = 0$ is relative to the data. A good group-discussion prompt: if we
measured dose so that $x = 0$ fell in the middle of the data, what would
the surface look like? (Part 2 answers this.)

## Part 2: Curvature with two parameters

**2a.**

> Compute $\text{SE}_1$, $r$, and $\text{SE}_2$, and the approximate 95%
> interval $\hat b \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$ for each (use
> $\hat b = `r b_used`$). Which do you think better characterizes our
> uncertainty about $b$, and why? Relate your answer to Part 1.

**Answer.**
$\text{SE}_1 = 1/\sqrt{0.145} = `r f2(se1_c)`$;
$r = 1.26/\sqrt{58.5 \times 0.145} = `r f2(r_c, 3)`$;
$\text{SE}_2 = `r f2(se1_c)`/\sqrt{1 - `r f2(r_c, 3)`^2} = `r f2(se2_c)`$.
Intervals: `r f2(int1_c, 1)[1]` to `r f2(int1_c, 1)[2]` using
$\text{SE}_1$; `r f2(int2_c, 1)[1]` to `r f2(int2_c, 1)[2]` using
$\text{SE}_2$. $\text{SE}_2$ is the better description of uncertainty:
its interval is close to the profile interval from 1a
(`r f2(prof_int[1], 1)` to `r f2(prof_int[2], 1)`).

**Why.** $\text{SE}_1$ uses only the curvature along the $b$ axis, with
$a'$ held fixed: it is the quadratic version of the slice.
$\text{SE}_2$ accounts for the fact that $a'$ can shift to compensate
when $b$ moves, as the profile does. The correction factor
$1/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ is always at least 1, so ignoring the correlation can
only make us overconfident. (For two parameters, $\text{SE}_2$ is what
`sqrt(diag(solve(H)))` returns; with the unrounded Hessian it is
`r f2(se_exact)`.)

**Watch for.** Sign of $r$: $H_{ab}$ is negative, so $r$ is positive
(`r f2(r_c, 3)`). Getting the sign wrong doesn't change $\text{SE}_2$
because $r$ is squared, but it's worth checking. Students who pick
$\text{SE}_1$ "because it's simpler" or "because it's smaller, so more
precise" are the ones to talk to: smaller isn't better if it ignores real
uncertainty.

**2b.**

> For the original, uncentered fit, $H_{bb} = 185$ and $r = -0.99968$.
> Compute both standard errors and their intervals again. Compare them
> with your slice and profile intervals from 1a, and with your answers
> to 2a. Centering didn't change the fitted curve, so what did it
> change?

**Answer.** $\text{SE}_1 = 1/\sqrt{185} = `r f2(se1_u, 4)`$, interval
`r f2(int1_u)[1]` to `r f2(int1_u)[2]`. $\text{SE}_2 =
`r f2(se1_u, 4)`/\sqrt{1 - 0.99968^2} = `r f2(se2_u)`$, interval
`r f2(int2_u, 1)[1]` to `r f2(int2_u, 1)[2]`. The $\text{SE}_1$ interval
matches the slice from 1a; the $\text{SE}_2$ interval is close to the
profile, and $\text{SE}_2$ is essentially the same as in 2a.

Centering changed the **shape and tilt of the surface** (correlation
`r f2(r_exact_u, 4)` before, `r f2(r_exact_c, 2)` after) and the meaning
of the intercept ($a'$ is the log-odds of death at $x = 1.8$, about 63
mg/L, inside the data). It did not change the fitted curve, the maximum
likelihood, $\hat b$, or the honest uncertainty in $b$.

**Why.** $\text{SE}_1$ depends on how the model is written (it
changes by a factor of about `r round(se2_u / se1_u)` here), so it
can't be a property of what the data say about $b$. $\text{SE}_2$ and the
profile describe the same quantity either way. The inflation factor
$1/\sqrt{1 - r^2} \approx `r round(1 / sqrt(1 - 0.99968^2))`$ is the
numerical version of the near-point slice in 1a.

**Watch for.** Rounding $r$ to $-0.9997$ or $-1$ before squaring: with
$r = -0.9997$, $\text{SE}_2$ comes out near 3.0; with $r = -1$ it's
undefined. Worth pointing out that when estimates are this correlated,
the arithmetic becomes touchy, which is one practical reason to center.
Some students will also say centering "made $b$ more precise"; it didn't,
it only made $\text{SE}_1$ less misleading.

**Discussion point (optional).** A thin, tilted valley is also hard for
optimizers to walk down, so centering or rescaling predictors often
helps fitting as well. This comes back when we cover optimization.

## Group discussion and revision

No fixed answer. The most useful disagreements are likely to be in 1b
(what $a$ means and why it trades off with $b$) and in 2a (why the
smaller standard error isn't the better one). Look for reflections that
connect the slice/profile picture in Part 1 to $\text{SE}_1$/$\text{SE}_2$
in Part 2.
